title: What can we gain from modelling complex hybrid incompatibilities?
content:
Abstract
Speciation occurs when populations become reproductively isolated. The contribution of intrinsic postzygotic incompatibilities to the build-up of reproductive isolation during the speciation process and their effectiveness as an isolating barrier upon secondary contact are contentious. Although the century-old (Bateson–)Dobzhansky–Muller model is widely accepted as an explanation for the existence of intrinsic hybrid incompatibilities, theory predicts that the resulting incompatibilities are poor barriers to gene flow. This is because the fitness landscape underlying this model does not necessarily contain a fitness valley. Highlighting empirical evidence and theoretical studies of complex hybrid incompatibilities, here we argue how models of multi-locus hybrid incompatibilities, which incorporate tunable epistasis and dominance, may challenge existing theoretical predictions and improve our understanding of the short- and long-term consequences of hybridization.
